prompt: What structural information does UV spectroscopy give?

choices.text: The nature of any conjugated π electron system
The molecular size and formula
choices.why: That is what mass spectrometry gives.

choices.text: The functional groups present
choices.why: That is what IR spectroscopy gives.

choices.text: The carbon–hydrogen framework
choices.why: That is what NMR spectroscopy gives.

explanation: Mass spectrometry, IR and NMR spectroscopy apply to all organic molecules. Ultraviolet spectroscopy is applicable only to conjugated compounds and gives information about conjugated π electron systems.

prompt: Which part of the ultraviolet region is of greatest interest to organic chemists?

choices.text: 200 to 400 nm
400 to 800 nm
choices.why: The UV region ends at 400 nm (4 × 10^−7 m), the short-wavelength end of the visible region. Longer wavelengths are not UV.

choices.text: 10 to 200 nm
choices.why: These shorter wavelengths are UV too, but the narrow range of greatest interest runs from 2 × 10^−7 m to 4 × 10^−7 m.

choices.text: 2 to 4 nm
choices.why: 2 × 10^−7 m is 200 nm, not 2 nm, because 1 nm = 10^−9 m.

explanation: The UV region runs from 4 × 10^−7 m (the short-wavelength end of the visible region) to 10^−8 m (the long-wavelength end of the X-ray region). The narrow range from 2 × 10^−7 m to 4 × 10^−7 m, or 200 to 400 nm, is of greatest interest to organic chemists.

prompt: 1,3-Butadiene absorbs at λ_max = 217 nm. Given that 1 nm = 10^−9 m, what is this wavelength in meters?
explanation: 217 nm × 10^−9 m/nm = 2.17 × 10^−7 m, inside the 2 × 10^−7 m to 4 × 10^−7 m range of interest.

prompt: When a conjugated molecule absorbs UV radiation, what does the absorbed energy do?

choices.text: It promotes an electron from a lower-energy orbital to a higher-energy one
It increases molecular vibrations
choices.why: That is what absorbed IR radiation does.

choices.text: It moves an electron from an antibonding orbital down to a bonding one
choices.why: Absorbed energy promotes the electron upward, from a bonding π orbital to an antibonding π* orbital.

choices.text: It breaks a π bond to give two radicals
choices.why: UV absorption promotes one electron to a higher-energy orbital; no bond is broken to form radicals.

explanation: With IR irradiation, the energy absorbed increases molecular vibrations. With UV radiation, the energy absorbed is the amount needed to promote an electron from a lower-energy orbital to a higher-energy one in a conjugated molecule.

prompt: When 1,3-butadiene absorbs UV light, between which orbitals is an electron promoted?

choices.text: From ψ_2 (the HOMO) to ψ_3* (the LUMO)
From ψ_1 to ψ_2
choices.why: Both are bonding orbitals and both are already full. The electron goes from the HOMO, ψ_2, to the LUMO, ψ_3*.

choices.text: From ψ_1 to ψ_4*
choices.why: The excitation goes from the highest occupied orbital to the lowest unoccupied one: ψ_2 to ψ_3*.

choices.text: From ψ_3* (the HOMO) to ψ_4* (the LUMO)
choices.why: ψ_3* is empty in the ground state, so it is the LUMO. The HOMO is ψ_2.

explanation: 1,3-Butadiene's two bonding π MOs are occupied and its two antibonding MOs are empty. UV excitation promotes an electron from ψ_2, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO), to ψ_3*, the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) (Figure 14.7.2).

prompt: Why is the UV excitation of 1,3-butadiene called a π → π* excitation?

choices.text: An electron goes from a bonding π MO to an antibonding π* MO
An electron goes from an antibonding π* MO to a bonding π MO
choices.why: Absorbing energy moves the electron up, from bonding to antibonding.

choices.text: A π bond is converted into a σ bond
choices.why: No bonds are rearranged. One electron moves to a higher-energy orbital.

choices.text: An electron goes from a σ orbital to a π orbital
choices.why: Both orbitals involved are π orbitals: bonding π to antibonding π*.

explanation: Because the electron is promoted from a bonding π molecular orbital to an antibonding π* molecular orbital, the transition is called a π → π* excitation ("pi to pi star"). For 1,3-butadiene it takes UV light of 217 nm.

prompt: In the definition of absorbance, A = log(I_0/I), what are I_0 and I?

choices.text: I_0 is the intensity of the incident light; I is the intensity transmitted through the sample
I_0 is the intensity transmitted through the sample; I is the intensity of the incident light
choices.why: Reversed: I_0 is the light going in and I is the light that gets through.

choices.text: I_0 is the intensity at λ_max; I is the intensity at any other wavelength
choices.why: Both are measured at the same wavelength: incident versus transmitted light.

choices.text: I_0 is the sample concentration; I is the path length
choices.why: Concentration and path length appear in the molar absorptivity equation, ε = A/(c × l).

explanation: Absorbance is defined as A = log(I_0/I), where I_0 is the intensity of the incident light and I is the intensity of the light transmitted through the sample.

prompt: A sample lets through only 1% of the incident UV light at λ_max, so I_0/I = 100. What is its absorbance?
How does the way a UV spectrum is displayed differ from an IR spectrum?

choices.text: UV spectra have the baseline at the bottom, so a peak shows an absorption
UV spectra have the baseline at the top, so a valley shows an absorption
choices.why: That is how IR spectra are usually displayed.

choices.text: UV spectra plot absorbance against concentration instead of wavelength
choices.why: A UV spectrum plots wavelength versus absorbance.

choices.text: There is no difference; both show absorptions as valleys
choices.why: Only IR spectra show absorptions as valleys. UV spectra show them as peaks.

explanation: For historical reasons, IR spectra put the zero-absorption baseline across the top of the chart, so a valley indicates an absorption. UV spectra put the baseline at the bottom, so a peak indicates an absorption.

prompt: Which statement about molar absorptivity (ε) is correct?

choices.text: It is a physical constant, characteristic of the substance's π electron system
It rises as the sample concentration rises
choices.why: Absorbance rises with concentration, but ε = A/(c × l) stays constant for a given substance.

choices.text: It depends on the length of the sample cell
choices.why: Path length is divided out in ε = A/(c × l). ε is characteristic of the compound.

choices.text: It has units of mol/L
choices.why: Its units are L/(mol · cm), usually dropped. Mol/L is the unit of concentration.

explanation: Molar absorptivity, ε = A/(c × l), is a physical constant, characteristic of the particular substance being observed and so of its π electron system. Its units, L/(mol · cm), are usually dropped.

prompt: What range of molar absorptivity (ε) is typical for conjugated dienes?

choices.why: That is about a thousand times too small. Conjugated dienes absorb strongly, with ε = 10,000 to 25,000.
Typical values for conjugated dienes are far larger: 10,000 to 25,000.

choices.text: About 138,000
choices.why: That is the molar absorptivity of β-carotene, not a typical conjugated diene.

explanation: Typical molar absorptivities for conjugated dienes are in the range ε = 10,000 to 25,000 L/(mol · cm), with the units usually dropped.

prompt: A conjugated diene at 4.0 × 10^−5 mol/L in a 1.00 cm cell has absorbance A = 0.84 at its λ_max. What is its molar absorptivity, ε, in L/(mol · cm)?
explanation: ε = A/(c × l) = 0.84 / (4.0 × 10^−5 mol/L × 1.00 cm) = 21,000 L/(mol · cm), inside the typical range of 10,000 to 25,000 for conjugated dienes.

prompt: β-Carotene has ε = 138,000 L/(mol · cm). A sample in a cell with a 1.0 cm path length has a UV absorbance of 0.37. What is the β-carotene concentration, in mol/L?
explanation: c = A/(ε × l) = 0.37 / (1.38 × 10^5 L/(mol · cm) × 1.0 cm) = 2.7 × 10^−6 mol/L. Rearranging ε = A/(c × l) this way lets you measure a concentration when A, ε and l are known.

prompt: Pure vitamin A has λ_max = 325 nm and ε = 50,100. A sample has A = 0.735 at 325 nm in a 1.00 cm cell. What is its vitamin A concentration, in mol/L, to three significant figures?
A conjugated diene has ε = 20,000. What absorbance would a 2.5 × 10^−5 mol/L solution of it give in a 1.00 cm cell?
Using E = (1.20 × 10^−4 kJ/mol)/λ, with λ in meters, what is the energy of 400 nm UV radiation, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 400 nm = 4.00 × 10^−7 m, so E = (1.20 × 10^−4 kJ/mol)/(4.00 × 10^−7) = 300 kJ/mol. At 200 nm the energy is 600 kJ/mol, so the UV range of interest spans 300–600 kJ/mol (Exercise 14.7.1).

prompt: Using E = (1.20 × 10^−4 kJ/mol)/λ, with λ in meters, how much energy does the 217 nm light that excites 1,3-butadiene carry, to the nearest kJ/mol?
explanation: 217 nm = 2.17 × 10^−7 m, so E = (1.20 × 10^−4 kJ/mol)/(2.17 × 10^−7) = 553 kJ/mol, within the 300–600 kJ/mol span of the 200–400 nm UV range.

prompt: How does the energy of UV radiation in the 200–400 nm range compare with the energies used in IR and NMR spectroscopy?

choices.text: UV energy is greater than both
UV energy is less than both
choices.why: UV radiation (300–600 kJ/mol) is more energetic than the radiation used in IR or NMR.

choices.text: UV energy lies between the IR and NMR energies
choices.why: UV radiation carries more energy than both IR and NMR radiation.

choices.text: All three use about the same energy
choices.why: UV energy (300–600 kJ/mol) is greater than IR or NMR energy.

explanation: The 200–400 nm range corresponds to 300–600 kJ/mol, more energy than is involved in IR or NMR spectroscopy (Exercise 14.7.1). That is enough to promote an electron to a higher orbital rather than just increase vibrations.

prompt: What is λ_max in a UV spectrum?

choices.text: The wavelength at the top of the absorption peak
The longest wavelength the instrument can measure
choices.why: λ_max marks the position of the absorption peak, not an instrument limit.

choices.text: The wavelength at which the absorbance is zero
choices.why: λ_max is where the absorbance is greatest, at the top of the peak.

choices.text: The largest molar absorptivity any compound can have
choices.why: That would be a value of ε. λ_max is a wavelength.

explanation: Unlike IR and NMR spectra, UV spectra are usually quite simple, often a single broad peak. Its position is given by the wavelength at the top of the peak, λ_max ("lambda max"); for 1,3-butadiene, λ_max = 217 nm.

prompt: Between which neighboring regions of the electromagnetic spectrum does the ultraviolet region lie?

choices.text: Between the visible region (at 4 × 10^−7 m) and the X-ray region (at 10^−8 m)
Between the visible region (at 10^−8 m) and the X-ray region (at 4 × 10^−7 m)
choices.why: The values are swapped. The visible region begins at 4 × 10^−7 m; the X-ray region begins at 10^−8 m.

choices.text: Between the visible region and the infrared region
choices.why: Infrared lies beyond the long-wavelength end of the visible region. UV lies on the short-wavelength side.

choices.text: Between the near-infrared and infrared regions
choices.why: Those regions lie at longer wavelengths than visible light. UV lies at shorter wavelengths.

explanation: The ultraviolet region extends from the short-wavelength end of the visible region (4 × 10^−7 m) to the long-wavelength end of the X-ray region (10^−8 m) (Figure 14.7.1).
